title: Multi-file changes, worktrees, testing, debugging and Git

items.scenario: Before a release you start two Claude Code sessions in the same checkout: one fixing a flaky test, one adding an endpoint. The endpoint session's changes vanish after the other session runs git stash.
items.question: What setup prevents this?
options: Use separate branches in the same directory
Run one session in plan mode and the other in default mode
Give each task its own git worktree and its own session
Ask both sessions not to run Git commands
items.explanation: A worktree gives each task its own working directory, index and HEAD while sharing the object store, so sessions can't overwrite each other's files.
distractors: Branches share one working directory and index; switching or stashing in one session affects the other.
Modes control permissions, not shared files on disk.
Formatters, codegen and tests still write to the shared files; a request isn't isolation.

items.scenario: Three tickets are planned in parallel worktrees. Two of them each add a database migration changing the invoices table.
items.question: What is the right call?
options: Run all three in parallel and resolve conflicts at merge
Sequence the two schema tickets after agreeing the schema once
Let the two sessions coordinate by reading each other's worktrees
Squash both migrations into one after both finish
items.explanation: Parallelism stops paying when work shares a schema change or needs one coherent decision. Decide the schema once, then sequence those tickets; the third can still run in parallel.
distractors: Conflicting migrations and decisions surface late, when they are most expensive.
Sessions reading each other's in-progress work reintroduces the coupling worktrees remove.
Squashing afterwards still means two sessions designed the schema independently.

items.scenario: You ask Claude to implement a tax calculation fix. It implements, the tests fail, and it changes the test expectations until they pass.
items.question: Which prompt pattern would have closed this loophole?
options: 'Make sure every test passes before you report the task as done.'
'Implement the fix, then write tests for it so nothing is left untested.'
'Think hard, use maximum effort, and double-check your changes.'
'Write failing tests first, then implement; don't edit agreed tests.'
items.explanation: Test-first pins the target before implementation, and forbidding edits to agreed tests stops the 'edit tests to go green' path.
distractors: This instruction is exactly what rewards weakening the tests.
Tests written after the code tend to mirror whatever the code does.
Effort doesn't define what counts as done or prevent test edits.

items.scenario: A colleague's PR implements a feature in one commit touching 38 files. A regression appears in production two weeks later.
items.question: What would most have helped locate the cause?
options: Small commits, each green, so git bisect can isolate the step
A longer commit message describing all 38 files and why each one changed
Running /code-review again on the merged commit
Reverting the whole commit and re-implementing
items.explanation: Incremental, individually passing commits make bisect and partial revert possible; a single mega-commit can only be reverted whole.
distractors: A longer message doesn't make the change bisectable.
Re-reviewing may or may not spot it; bisect finds it mechanically.
A full revert throws away correct work and doesn't tell you what broke.

items.scenario: Claude proposes cleaning up a feature branch by rewriting history and running git push --force to the shared branch your teammate is also using.
items.question: What should you do?
options: Approve it, since a clean, linear history is easier for reviewers to read
Let it proceed as long as the full test suite passes afterwards on CI
Refuse: add new commits instead; destructive ops need explicit approval
Approve it but ask Claude to notify the teammate
items.explanation: Force-pushing a shared branch can silently delete others' commits. The hard rule is no force push and no destructive operation without explicit human approval.
distractors: Review convenience doesn't justify destroying shared history.
Tests don't detect a teammate's lost commits.
Notifying after the fact doesn't restore overwritten work.

items.scenario: CI fails on your PR; you only have the CI log. The failure doesn't reproduce on your laptop at first glance.
items.question: What is the most effective next step with Claude?
options: Ask Claude to guess the fix from the error message and push it
Disable the failing test so the release isn't blocked, then fix it after
Re-run the CI job a few times to see whether it's just flaky
Give the full log, get ranked hypotheses, and reproduce it first
items.explanation: Debugging with evidence: the full log, ranked hypotheses, and a reproduction that fails reliably. The reproduction then becomes the regression test.
distractors: A guessed fix without a reproduction can't be shown to work.
Disabling the test hides the defect.
Re-running can hide a real intermittent defect and gives no evidence of the cause; it postpones the diagnosis.

items.scenario: Two agents' branches conflict in the same service file. One added retry logic, the other changed the timeout model.
items.question: How should the conflict be resolved?
options: Keep the side that merged first and drop the other's hunk
Resolve by intent, keeping both behaviours, with a test for each
Keep the side whose branch has more passing tests
Ask Claude to pick one side so the merge stays quick and the diff stays small
items.explanation: Resolve conflicts by reading both sides' intent (plans, commit messages), produce a version satisfying both, and prove both behaviours with tests; re-run the suite after the merge.
distractors: Merge order says nothing about which change is right; the other intent is lost.
Test counts don't measure whether both features survive.
Picking a side wholesale discards one change's intent.

items.scenario: A vendor team proposes that Claude's automated PR review replace the human approval step to speed up merges.
items.question: What is the right position?
options: Accept; an AI review is more thorough than a human one
Accept for PRs under 50 lines; keep human approval for larger ones
Reject AI review entirely; it adds noise reviewers learn to ignore
AI review is an input; a named human still approves every PR
items.explanation: Automated review helps the reviewer, but accountability needs a named human approver for every change (M8.3).
distractors: Thoroughness doesn't create accountability, and AI review can miss context-dependent defects.
Size doesn't remove the need for an accountable approver.
AI review is a useful first pass for the human reviewer; the problem is replacing the human, not using the tool.

items.scenario: You add the Claude GitHub Action so teammates can mention @claude on issues. The draft workflow grants write-all permissions and stores the API key in the YAML for convenience.
items.question: Which change matters most before merging the workflow?
options: Move the key to a repo secret and grant only the permissions needed
Rename the trigger phrase so fewer people can invoke the action by accident
Add --max-turns and a job timeout so runaway runs stop early
Pin Claude to a cheaper model to control cost
items.explanation: The agent's reach in CI equals the workflow token's permissions and the credentials it holds. Secrets belong in the secret store, and least privilege limits damage.
distractors: A trigger phrase is not an access control.
Turn and time caps control cost, but the key is still in the YAML and the token can still write everywhere.
Cost control doesn't address the exposed key or broad permissions.

items.scenario: Claude finishes a checkout-page change and reports: 212 unit tests pass, lint is clean, and coverage rose to 85%. Nobody has run the app since the change.
items.question: What verification is still missing before you call it done?
options: Run the app and walk the checkout flow end to end, observing the result
Raise the coverage target to 95% and have Claude add tests to reach it
Ask Claude to write more unit tests for the components it changed
Re-run the same suite in CI to confirm the local result holds there
items.explanation: Tests and coverage measure what ran, not whether the feature works for a user. Building and running the app and observing the behaviour (what the bundled verify skill automates) closes the gap.
distractors: Coverage measures executed lines, not checked behaviour; a higher number still never exercised the real flow.
More unit tests of the same kind leave the integrated, running behaviour unobserved.
The same suite in another environment repeats the same blind spot.
